title: Prompt inoculation field journal
content:
Goal: experiment with a lightweight prompt "inoculation" pattern — prepend small structured salts that bias the model away from overconfident fabrication while preserving brevity and helpfulness.

Context / motivation:
- We keep seeing hallucination spikes when the model is asked about obscure factual minutiae (dates, internal feature flags, historical ticket numbers). Teams want a cheap prompting pattern to reduce hallucination without adding heavy verification steps or external tool calls.
- Idea: insert a 1–3 sentence inoculation layer before user instructions that sets expectations, provides a short verification heuristic, and offers a constrained response format. The layer is intentionally terse to avoid large token overhead.

Hypothesis:
- A short inoculation salt will reduce outright fabrications by nudging the model toward prefacing uncertain answers with hedges or refusing when unsupported.
- Side-effects may include higher abstention, slightly longer responses (explanations/hard refusals), and small token overhead.

Quick experiment plan (micro-bench):
- Dataset: 20 crowd-sourced obscure-fact Qs (internal names, obscure API version numbers, old PR numbers, edge-case policy dates).
- Models: rwi-2-70B-quant (hosted), rwi-1-13B (hosted) — both with streaming disabled for consistent decode.
- Conditions: base prompt (no inoculation) vs inoculation-A (heuristic salt) vs inoculation-B (strong-refusal salt) vs inoculation-C (few-shot + salt).
- Metrics: hallucination_rate (binary judged), hedging_rate (explicit hedge token presence), avg_tokens, answer_helpfulness (0–3 rubric), latency (ms).

Inoculation variants (templates):
- base: "Answer succinctly."
- inoc-A (light): "If you are not sure, say 'I don't know' rather than invent details. Try to provide relevant context if available. Answer succinctly."
- inoc-B (refuse-strong): "If the model cannot assert a fact with high confidence, reply 'Cannot verify' and suggest a simple way to check. Avoid making up numbers or names. Answer succinctly."
- inoc-C (few-shot seeding): include 2 brief examples showing a correct answer and a correct refusal:
  Example 1 Q: 'When did feature X ship?' A: 'Feature X shipped in 2023 (approx). Confirm in release notes.'
  Example 2 Q: 'What was PR #587 about?' A: 'Cannot verify — recommend searching repo history.'
  + then the same instruction to be concise.

Sample few-shot set (inoc-C examples):
- Q: "When was the telemetry client added?"
  A: "Cannot verify — check CHANGELOG.md in main repo."
- Q: "What is the internal flag name used for rollout?"
  A: "Cannot verify; recommend checking infra/flags or asking infra owner."

Early observations (manual run, 2025-11-20):
- rwi-2-70B base hallucination_rate: 0.55 (11/20 fabricated specific numbers/names); hedging_rate: 0.10
- inoc-A reduced hallucination to 0.40 but increased hedging to 0.28; answer_helpfulness improved slightly for partials (0.9 -> 1.1 median).
- inoc-B dropped hallucination to 0.18 but many answers were 'Cannot verify' (abstention). Users complained in quick qualitative read of answers: "too many refusals for things we expect simple answers to."
- inoc-C performed best on precision (0.85 non-hallucinated when answered) but had mixed recall/coverage: the model resisted making borderline inferences.

Failure cases spotted:
- The model sometimes treats the inoculation salt as an additional instruction to be creative: e.g., after inoc-A it would say "I think it was 2019" with hedge tokens but still invent. Hedge alone isn't always enough.
- When user tasks want plausible-sounding synthesis (e.g., summarizing a noisy thread), inoculation causes over-abstention.
- Few-shot examples must be extremely tightly matched to target domain; divergent examples can confuse the model and make it pick the wrong refusal style.

Prompt text bank (current candidates):
- SALT-1: "If you cannot be certain, say 'I don't know' or 'Cannot verify'. Don't invent numbers or names. If you can give a direction for checking, include one short suggestion. Now answer the question briefly."
- SALT-2: "Only provide facts you can be confident in; mark any speculation with 'likely' or 'approx'. Prefer to recommend verifiable next steps rather than guessing."
- SALT-3 (concise): "Prefer 'Cannot verify' over fabricating. If possible, give a one-line check step."

Experimental prompts (full):
- Example prompt for test run A:
  [SALT-1]
  Q: "What is the internal metric name for request latency SLO?"

- Example prompt for test run B:
  [SALT-3]
  Few-shot examples:
   - Q: "When did feature Y land?" A: "Cannot verify; check internal release notes."
   - Q: "Who is owner of component Z?" A: "Cannot verify; check owners.md."
  Q: "What was PR #402 about?"

Notes-to-self / heuristics learned:
- Keep salt token count under ~25 tokens if possible; beyond that we start to eat too much token budget and user-visible latency increases.
- Combine inoculation with a short deterministic format hint: e.g., "If you answer, start with a one-line claim and one-line source." That encourages brief answers + source pointers.
- For developer-facing tool (CLI or internal bot), stronger inoculation (inoc-B) is acceptable because users prefer accuracy and can follow links. For consumer-facing UIs, inoc-A or inoc-C + post-hoc verification is better.

Next experiments (planned):
- Larger micro-bench (200 Qs) with stratified taxonomy: API names, PR numbers, dates, personnel, internal flag names.
- A/B test with Redwood Console integ — one route using inoc-A vs control to measure product impact on support tickets (if possible).
- Combine inoculation with lightweight retrieval: salt instructs model to try to answer, but if low-confidence, call a fast retrieval over CHANGELOG and return a cite. Measure hybrid token+latency tradeoffs.

Open questions / risks:
- Is inoculation just creating a style-of-response that looks safer, while allowing subtle fabrications inside 'likely' phrasing? Need a robust annotation rubric distinguishing safe hedging from deceptive hedging.
- Will repeated use of inoculation create brittle behavior when combined with tool-calls or function-calling? (Check interplay with our function-calling system.)
- How to surface to customer: simple 'safety salt' toggle per route vs baked into model serving policy?

Draft small internal blurb for a solutions note (copyable):
"We are trialing a low-cost prompting technique called 'inoculation' that reduces hallucination by instructing the model to prefer abstention and suggest verifiable next steps. Early micro-benchmarks show a ~35% reduction in outright fabrications for our test set with moderate increase in hedging. Next steps include a larger benchmark and measuring customer-facing impact."

Quick raw examples (copied from run logs):
- Q: "What was the version number that enabled X?"
  base: "It was 2.4.1."  (fabricated)
  SALT-1: "Cannot verify; check CHANGELOG.md for exact version."

- Q: "Who merged PR #213?"
  base: "Samir Patel" (fabricated)
  SALT-3: "Cannot verify; search PR history or git blame to confirm."

Closing thought: inoculation feels promising as a low-friction tool in the prompt engineering toolkit — especially for internal agents and developer-facing UIs. The key is controlling for over-abstention and ensuring hedges are honest (not a rhetorical cover for invention). Keep this doc as the working scratchpad; push the 200-sample benchmark results here when ready.
